subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What does the term 'urbanisation' mean?
options: The increase in the proportion of a country's population living in towns and cities
The movement of people from cities back to the countryside
The growth of farming and agriculture in rural areas
The decrease in the total population of a country
questions.explain: Urbanisation is the rising share of a population living in urban areas rather than rural ones.

questions.q: A 'megacity' is usually defined as an urban area with a population of at least how many people?
options: 10 million
1 million
5 million
50 million
questions.explain: A megacity is conventionally defined as a city with a population of over 10 million people.

questions.q: Which of the following is a 'push' factor that drives rural-urban migration?
options: Crop failure and rural poverty
Better-paid jobs in the city
More schools and hospitals in the city
Higher wages in factories
questions.explain: Push factors, such as poverty and poor harvests, drive people away from rural areas.

questions.q: Which of the following is a 'pull' factor attracting people to cities?
options: A wider range of jobs and higher wages
Drought affecting local farmland
Lack of services in the countryside
Conflict in a rural region
questions.explain: Pull factors, such as jobs and better services, attract migrants towards urban areas.

questions.q: The movement of people from the countryside to towns and cities is known as:
options: Rural-urban migration
Counter-urbanisation
Suburbanisation
International migration
questions.explain: Rural-urban migration is the movement of people from rural areas into towns and cities.

questions.q: Why are the fastest rates of urbanisation today found in low-income countries (LICs) and newly emerging economies (NEEs)?
options: Rapid economic development and high rural-urban migration draw people to growing cities
Their populations are shrinking so cities grow relatively larger
They already have very high proportions of urban dwellers
Governments force rural people to remain on farms
questions.explain: In LICs and NEEs, industrialisation and rural-urban migration are driving very rapid urban growth.

questions.q: Besides migration, what is the other main cause of rapid urban population growth in many cities?
options: Natural increase, as birth rates exceed death rates
Falling life expectancy in cities
Emigration of young people abroad
A decline in the total national population
questions.explain: Natural increase (more births than deaths) adds to urban populations alongside inward migration.

questions.q: In high-income countries, why has the pace of urbanisation slowed compared with LICs?
options: A very high proportion of the population is already urban
Their cities have run out of space to grow
People are moving in large numbers to farms
Birth rates in cities are extremely high
questions.explain: HICs urbanised earlier, so most people already live in towns and cities, slowing further change.

questions.q: What term describes the unplanned, self-built housing areas that often develop on the edges of rapidly growing cities?
options: Squatter settlements
Central business districts
Greenbelt zones
Gated communities
questions.explain: Squatter settlements (informal settlements or slums) are unplanned, self-built areas housing the urban poor.

questions.q: Which of these is a common social challenge caused by rapid urban growth?
options: Not enough clean water and sanitation for all residents
Too much unused housing sitting empty
A shortage of people to fill available jobs
An excess of green open space
questions.explain: Rapid growth often outstrips the provision of clean water, sanitation and health services.

questions.q: The uncontrolled outward spread of a city into surrounding countryside is called:
options: Urban sprawl
Regeneration
Deindustrialisation
Urbanisation
questions.explain: Urban sprawl is the spreading of a city's built-up area outwards into rural land.

questions.q: Why does rapid urban growth often lead to increased traffic congestion and air pollution?
options: More people and vehicles concentrate in an area faster than transport infrastructure can cope
Fewer people use cars as cities grow
City authorities ban all public transport
Roads are widened faster than the population grows
questions.explain: Vehicle numbers rise faster than road and transport provision, causing congestion and pollution.

questions.q: Why are informal settlements often built in hazardous locations such as steep slopes or floodplains?
options: These are the only areas of unused land available to poor migrants
Wealthy residents prefer these sites
The land is the most expensive in the city
Governments provide free services there
questions.explain: Poor migrants settle on marginal, risky land because safer, serviced land is unaffordable or unavailable.

questions.q: How can rapid urban growth create economic challenges for a city?
options: High unemployment and underemployment develop when jobs cannot keep pace with population
There are always more jobs than people to fill them
Wages rise so high that businesses cannot form
The workforce becomes too small to support industry
questions.explain: When population grows faster than formal jobs, unemployment and low-paid informal work rise.

questions.q: Why is managing waste a major challenge in rapidly growing cities?
options: The volume of waste rises faster than collection and disposal services can handle
Cities produce very little waste as they grow
Recycling removes the need for any waste collection
Waste naturally decomposes before it can accumulate
questions.explain: Growing populations generate more waste than under-resourced services can collect and dispose of safely.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a 'sustainable city'?
options: A city that meets the needs of its residents today without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs
A city that grows as fast as possible regardless of environmental cost
A city with no industry or transport at all
A city where all residents own private cars
questions.explain: Sustainable urban living balances current social, economic and environmental needs with those of the future.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of using land sustainably within a city?
options: Building on brownfield (previously used) sites rather than greenfield land
Clearing greenbelt farmland for new housing estates
Draining wetlands for car parks
Replacing all parks with car showrooms
questions.explain: Reusing brownfield land protects countryside and greenfield sites from being built on.

questions.q: How does investing in integrated public transport help make a city more sustainable?
options: It reduces car use, easing congestion and lowering air pollution and carbon emissions
It encourages every resident to buy a private car
It increases traffic by removing bus and rail options
It has no effect on air quality
questions.explain: Efficient public transport cuts private car journeys, reducing congestion, pollution and emissions.

questions.q: Why are green spaces such as parks and urban trees important for a sustainable city?
options: They improve air quality, aid wellbeing and support wildlife and drainage
They increase air pollution in the city centre
They stop all economic activity from taking place
They are only useful for storing waste
questions.explain: Green spaces enhance air quality, biodiversity, drainage and residents' quality of life.

questions.q: A rapidly growing NEE city suffers from overflowing landfill and polluted rivers. Which measure would most improve environmental sustainability?
options: Introducing recycling schemes and improved waste and water treatment
Encouraging more single-use packaging
Dumping additional waste into the rivers
Closing all recycling centres to save money
questions.explain: Recycling and better waste and water treatment reduce pollution and manage resources sustainably.

questions.q: A young farmer leaves a drought-hit village after his crops fail, moving to the capital to seek factory work. Which factors best explain his move?
options: A push factor (crop failure) and a pull factor (city jobs)
Two pull factors only
Counter-urbanisation
Natural increase in the village
questions.explain: Crop failure pushes him from the countryside while city jobs pull him towards the capital.

questions.q: A city planner notes that new arrivals are building homes with no clean water, electricity or legal land rights. This is best described as the growth of:
options: Informal (squatter) settlements
A central business district
A sustainable eco-suburb
A greenbelt zone
questions.explain: Self-built housing lacking services and legal tenure characterises informal or squatter settlements.

questions.q: To cut carbon emissions and improve energy sustainability, which action should a city government prioritise?
options: Encouraging renewable energy and energy-efficient buildings
Subsidising more coal-fired power stations
Removing insulation from public buildings
Banning cycle lanes and bus routes
questions.explain: Renewable energy and energy efficiency lower carbon emissions and conserve resources.
